claims.claim: In a systematic review of capacity for treatment decisions in adult medical patients, MMSE scores below 20 made incapacity more likely, scores of 20 to 24 did not change the likelihood, and scores above 24 made incapacity less likely.
claims.supporting_passage: Although not designed to assess incapacity, Mini-Mental State Examination (MMSE) scores less than 20 increased the likelihood of incapacity (LR, 6.3; 95% CI, 3.7-11), scores of 20 to 24 had no effect (LR, 0.87; 95% CI, 0.53-1.2), and scores greater than 24 significantly lowered the likelihood of incapacity (LR, 0.14; 95% CI, 0.06-0.34). ... The MMSE is useful only at extreme scores.
claims.location: Abstract, Results and Conclusions
claims.pico_timeframe: Adult medicine patients without severe mental illness (review of 43 high-quality prospective studies) / MMSE score bands / reference standard capacity assessment / incapacity for medical treatment decisions / cross-sectional
claims.safe_wording: In a large review of studies of treatment decisions, an MMSE score below 20 made it more likely that a patient lacked capacity. A score of 20 to 24 did not change the likelihood either way. A score above 24 made it less likely. The authors concluded the MMSE is useful only at extreme scores.
claims.qualifications: Say 'decisions about treatment' (the studies were of treatment decisions in medical patients, not decisions about where to live). Say the MMSE was not designed to assess capacity. For practitioners the likelihood ratios (6.3, 0.87, 0.14) may be given; for the public say 'more likely', 'no change', 'less likely'. Do not convert the likelihood ratios into 'X times more likely' or into a probability without stating the starting probability.
claims.conflicting_or_uncertain: The 20 to 24 band confidence interval (0.53 to 1.2) is wide, so 'no information' means 'no clear shift' rather than a precise zero. Cut-offs are specific to the MMSE; no evidence was found in this batch for equivalent bands on MoCA or ACE-III, so the post should not transfer the numbers to other tests.

numbers.meaning: MMSE band; likelihood ratio 6.3 (95% CI 3.7 to 11) for incapacity
MMSE band; likelihood ratio 0.87 (95% CI 0.53 to 1.2), described by the authors as 'no effect'
MMSE band; likelihood ratio 0.14 (95% CI 0.06 to 0.34) for incapacity
high-quality prospective studies included in the review (not all contributed MMSE data)

claims.claim: A score above 24 lowers but does not rule out incapacity; a decision-specific assessment is still needed.
claims.supporting_passage: Sessums 2011: "scores greater than 24 significantly lowered the likelihood of incapacity (LR, 0.14; 95% CI, 0.06-0.34)"; "Evaluation of the capacity of a patient to make medical decisions should occur in the context of specific medical decisions when incapacity is considered." Orr and Baruah 2018: "This decision confirms that capacity is time-and decision-specific and can fluctuate." Poole 2014 (Discussion): "The MMSE neither determines residence capacity, nor any other specific capacity [41]."
claims.location: Sessums abstract (Context, Results); Orr 2018 full text ('Capacity: evolution of case law'); Poole 2014 full text, Discussion
claims.pico_timeframe: As C09-26-a; legal principle from UK educational review; authors' discussion statement in a UK dementia ethnography
claims.safe_wording: A high score lowers the chance that someone lacks capacity, but it does not rule it out. Capacity is judged one decision at a time, so a test score can prompt an assessment but can't replace it.
claims.qualifications: The judge asked for a link to executive impairment; the evidence opened here does not quantify how often people with high MMSE scores lack capacity because of executive problems (see C09-12-b on the thin evidence for the 'frontal lobe paradox'). Say 'can still lack capacity for a complex decision' as a reasoned point, not as a measured rate.
claims.conflicting_or_uncertain: None found against the principle. A worked post-test probability could be calculated from the 26% inpatient prevalence, but this mixes pooled figures and is not in the source; do not publish a calculated percentage.

numbers.meaning: likelihood ratio for incapacity with MMSE above 24 (95% CI 0.06 to 0.34); lowers, does not remove, the likelihood

claims.claim: In 37 patients with mild to moderate Alzheimer's disease, MMSE scores of 21 to 25 did not separate those with and without capacity well.
claims.supporting_passage: In this study of 37 patients with mild to moderate Alzheimer's disease, a fairly wide range of MMSE scores (21 to 25, which includes an often used cutoff for "normal") did not discriminate capacity status well.
claims.location: Abstract
claims.pico_timeframe: 37 people with mild to moderate Alzheimer's disease / MMSE score / capacity to consent to research / cross-sectional
claims.safe_wording: An earlier study of 37 people with Alzheimer's disease found the same pattern: scores of 21 to 25 did not reliably separate people who could consent from those who could not.
claims.qualifications: The decision studied was consent to research, not treatment; the sample was small. Use as corroboration, not as the headline.
claims.conflicting_or_uncertain: None found.

numbers.meaning: patients with mild to moderate Alzheimer's disease
MMSE range that did not discriminate capacity status well

claims.claim: Incapacity for treatment decisions was common among medical inpatients and often missed by clinicians; the Aid to Capacity Evaluation had useful test characteristics and is freely available.
claims.supporting_passage: Incapacity was uncommon in healthy elderly control participants (2.8%; 95% confidence interval [CI], 1.7%-3.9%) compared with medicine inpatients (26%; 95% CI, 18%-35%). Clinicians accurately diagnosed incapacity (positive likelihood ratio [LR+] of 7.9; 95% CI, 2.7-13), although they recognized it in only 42% (95% CI, 30%-53%) of affected patients. ... The ACE was validated in the largest study; it is freely available online and includes a training module.
claims.location: Abstract, Results
claims.pico_timeframe: Pooled prevalence of incapacity and clinician recognition across included studies; treatment decisions
claims.safe_wording: In the same review, about 1 in 4 medical inpatients lacked capacity for a treatment decision, and clinicians recognised it in about 4 in 10 of those patients. The Aid to Capacity Evaluation (ACE) had useful accuracy and is free to use.
claims.qualifications: Optional context. '26%' is a pooled estimate across studies with a wide interval (18% to 35%); 'about 1 in 4' is a fair plain reading. The 42% is recognition among patients who lacked capacity, not among all patients.
claims.conflicting_or_uncertain: Studies were mostly North American and up to 2011.

numbers.meaning: pooled prevalence of incapacity among medicine inpatients (95% CI 18% to 35%)
incapacity among healthy older control participants (95% CI 1.7% to 3.9%)
proportion of patients lacking capacity whom clinicians recognised (95% CI 30% to 53%)
Aid to Capacity Evaluation test characteristics

claims.claim: In CC v KK (Court of Protection, England and Wales, 2012) an 82-year-old woman with vascular dementia, Parkinson's disease and hemiplegia, whom several professionals had assessed as lacking capacity to decide where to live, was found by the judge to have that capacity.
claims.supporting_passage: Hughes 2015: "The case concerned an 82-year-old woman, KK, who had hemiplegia, Parkinson's disease and vascular dementia. She was totally dependent on others for her personal care, frequently sought help by the use of a telecare alarm service and showed considerable anxiety. Finally, she was admitted to a nursing home with dehydration and a urinary tract infection. But she wanted to return home. Her case involved a number of professionals assessing her capacity on a number of occasions. They all found that she lacked residence capacity, but Mr Justice Baker determined otherwise." Ruck Keene 2019: "One of the other cases in which the judge showed clear commitment to fully articulating and applying the functional conception of capacity (and in doing so, overruled expert evidence) was CC v KK [2012] EWCOP 2136, concerning the capacity of an elderly woman with dementia to make decisions about her residence and care."
claims.location: Hughes 2015 full text, 'Approaches to assessment: outcome v. functional'; Ruck Keene 2019 full text, Discussion
claims.pico_timeframe: Single first-instance judgment, Court of Protection, England and Wales, July 2012
claims.safe_wording: In a 2012 Court of Protection case in England, an 82-year-old woman with dementia wanted to go home from a nursing home. Professionals had repeatedly judged that she lacked capacity to decide where to live. The judge found that she had it.
claims.qualifications: One first-instance judgment in England and Wales; it binds no other court and Scotland has different legislation (Adults with Incapacity (Scotland) Act 2000). Say 'a judge found', not 'the law says'. Do not add details of her care or outcome beyond these sources.
claims.conflicting_or_uncertain: The judgment itself could not be opened; facts rest on two peer-reviewed secondary sources that agree.

numbers.meaning: KK's age
year of judgment

claims.claim: The judge said the person must be presented with detailed options so that their ability to weigh them can be fairly assessed.
claims.supporting_passage: Moreover, different individuals may give different weight to different factors; and capacity assessors should not start with a blank canvas: "The person under evaluation must be presented with detailed options so that their capacity to weigh up those options can be fairly assessed" (CC v KK, para 68).
claims.location: Ruck Keene 2019 full text, Discussion (quoting CC v KK para 68)
claims.pico_timeframe: Judicial statement, CC v KK [2012] EWHC 2136 (COP), para 68
claims.safe_wording: The judge said: "The person under evaluation must be presented with detailed options so that their capacity to weigh up those options can be fairly assessed."
claims.qualifications: Quote exactly as above and attribute to CC v KK, para 68 (as quoted in Ruck Keene et al 2019). Do not paraphrase as 'the law requires'.
claims.conflicting_or_uncertain: Same case also held (per Chiu 2017 in LSE Law Review, seen only as a search excerpt and not used) that the person need weigh only the salient details, not every detail. Consistent with Hughes 2015 quoting Heart of England v JB: 'a broad, general understanding'. The post may add that the person need not grasp every detail.

numbers.meaning: paragraph number of the judgment

claims.claim: For a decision about where to live, the information the person should be given includes why a move is proposed, the other options (for example home with extra help), and the likely consequences of each choice and of not deciding, stated honestly for the care home option too.
claims.supporting_passage: Box 4: "The person should know why a change of residence is being proposed ... The person should know what is being proposed (e.g. they should know that it is being suggested they should move into a care home) The person should be informed if there are other options (e.g. that they could go home but extra help is recommended because of the risks identified) The person should understand the likely consequences of making any particular decision, including a decision not to follow the advice being given, as well as the consequences of making no decision at all". Worked example: "an alternative would be for him to go home with professional carers coming in to see him several times a day; and he should understand that if he goes into a care home it might well become the place he lives permanently and, alternatively, if he goes home and accepts the care package it cannot be guaranteed that he will not run into similar problems again in the future." Statute as quoted: "The person will be unable to make the required decision if, owing to the impairment or disturbance, he or she is unable to understand, retain, use or weigh the relevant information or to communicate the decision (MCA: section 3)."
claims.location: Hughes 2015 full text, 'The ‘information’', Box 4 and vignette; 'Context' for MCA s3
claims.pico_timeframe: Expert recommendation for residence-capacity assessment under MCA 2005 (England and Wales)
claims.safe_wording: Specialists in residence capacity recommend telling the person why a move is suggested, what the other options are, such as going home with carers several times a day, and what each choice could mean. That includes saying plainly that a care home may become permanent, and that going home with help carries no guarantee.
claims.qualifications: This is an expert proposal in a peer-reviewed review, not the statute's wording; MCA s3(4) (reasonably foreseeable consequences) itself was not opened. Attribute as 'specialists recommend' or 'a review by residence-capacity researchers recommends'.
claims.conflicting_or_uncertain: None found.

claims.claim: On English hospital wards, professionals varied widely in what information they treated as relevant when assessing whether people with dementia could decide where to live, and legal standards were not routinely applied.
claims.supporting_passage: Abstract: "Our findings suggest that whilst professionals profess to be familiar with broad legal standards governing the assessment of capacity under the MCA, these standards are not routinely applied in practice in general hospital settings when assessing capacity to decide place of residence on discharge from hospital." Full text: "Our findings suggest that there is currently a wide inconsistency of approach amongst professionals when identifying 'information relevant to the decision' (section 3(1)(a) MCA) during the assessment of residence capacity." "Only by gathering this information can the assessor present the various options, alternatives and risks associated with a particular choice of residence to a patient so that they can understand and weigh those factors in the balance in order to demonstrate decisional capacity and make an informed choice."
claims.location: Abstract (Results); full text (accepted manuscript), Introduction and 'Understanding Information Relevant to the Decision'
claims.pico_timeframe: 29 cases of people with dementia on three wards, two NHS trusts, North of England / residence-capacity assessment in practice / compared with MCA standards / 2008 to 2009
claims.safe_wording: A study on English hospital wards found staff varied widely in what information they gave or tested when judging whether a person with dementia could decide where to live.
claims.qualifications: Qualitative, 29 cases, fieldwork 2008 to 2009 (before CC v KK). Give no percentages. Say 'a study found', not 'assessments usually fail'.
claims.conflicting_or_uncertain: Practice may have changed since 2009; no recent quantitative audit was found in this batch.

numbers.meaning: patient cases studied
fieldwork period

claims.claim: In video-recorded hospital capacity assessments, options were not always presented to the patient.
claims.supporting_passage: Variation from this structure was observed across the dataset, notably in the way in which options were (or were not) presented. ... One phase, option listing, varied in practice and options were not always presented.
claims.location: Abstract, Outcomes & Results; What this study adds
claims.pico_timeframe: Four video-recorded capacity assessments of hospital patients with communication difficulties after acquired brain injury / conversation analysis / England
claims.safe_wording: When researchers filmed four real capacity assessments in hospital, options were not always put to the patient.
claims.qualifications: Four recordings only, in acquired brain injury rather than older people or dementia. Use only as an illustration, never as a rate.
claims.conflicting_or_uncertain: Too small to generalise.

numbers.meaning: video-recorded capacity assessments analysed

claims.claim: In a review of 40 disputed Court of Protection capacity cases, in one the judge found the person had not been given relevant information about care options at home.
claims.supporting_passage: In one of these, the judge deemed P had not been provided with relevant information around care options at home.
claims.location: Ruck Keene 2019 full text, Results (support principle)
claims.pico_timeframe: 40 published capacity-dispute judgments, England and Wales, 2007 to 2017
claims.safe_wording: Courts have criticised assessments where the person was not told what care would be available at home.
claims.qualifications: Optional. One case among 40; do not present as frequent. The excerpt does not name the case.
claims.conflicting_or_uncertain: None.

numbers.meaning: disputed capacity cases reviewed

claims.claim: The judge warned that professionals may conflate capacity assessment with best interests and give more weight to the physical safety of a care home than to the emotional security of home.
claims.supporting_passage: In para. 65, he reiterated the point about the importance of the objective test of capacity being made without reference to what might be best for the person and emphasised again the saliency of home: 'There is, I perceive, a danger that professionals, including judges, may objectively conflate a capacity assessment with a best interests analysis and conclude that the person under review should attach greater weight to the physical security and comfort of a residential home and less importance to the emotional security and comfort that the person derives from being in their own home'.
claims.location: Hughes 2015 full text, 'Approaches to assessment: outcome v. functional'
claims.pico_timeframe: Judicial statement, CC v KK para 65
claims.safe_wording: The same judge warned that professionals can slip from asking 'can she decide?' into 'what is best for her?', and then expect the person to value a care home's safety over the security of being at home.
claims.qualifications: Optional. If quoted, use the exact words above with para 65.
claims.conflicting_or_uncertain: None.

numbers.meaning: paragraph number

claims.claim: About 1 in 3 people in hospital after a stroke have aphasia.
claims.supporting_passage: Median frequencies for mixed stroke (ischemic and hemorrhagic) were 30% and 34% for acute and rehabilitation settings, respectively. Frequencies by stroke type were lowest for acute subarachnoid hemorrhage (9%) and highest for acute ischemic stroke (62%) when arrival to the hospital was ≤3 hours from stroke onset. Articles monitoring aphasia for 1 year demonstrated aphasia frequencies 2% to 12% lower than baseline.
claims.location: Abstract, Results
claims.pico_timeframe: Unselected adult stroke patients in trials or consecutive cohorts / frequency of aphasia / acute and rehabilitation settings / up to 1 year
claims.safe_wording: About 1 in 3 people in hospital after a stroke have aphasia, a difficulty with understanding or using language.
claims.qualifications: 30% (acute) and 34% (rehabilitation) are median frequencies across studies of mixed stroke; frequency varies widely by stroke type and timing and falls somewhat over the first year.
claims.conflicting_or_uncertain: Range across settings 9% to 62%; say 'about 1 in 3' only for hospital stroke populations in general.

numbers.meaning: median frequency of aphasia in acute settings, mixed stroke
median frequency in rehabilitation settings, mixed stroke
range of frequencies by stroke type and setting

claims.claim: Aphasia is a disorder of language; it can hide a person's ability to decide, and some people with aphasia also have other cognitive problems, so aphasia alone does not show that the person lacks capacity or that they have it.
claims.supporting_passage: Stipinovich 2023: "The presence of neurological pathology, for example, aphasia, and its associated difficulties with language and/or cognition, may affect an individual's capacity to make decisions, or their ability to reveal their capacity to make decisions." Kim 2020: "Because people with aphasia (PWA) have impaired language abilities and may also present with cognitive deficits, they may have difficulty during decision-making tasks." Hughes 2015 (Box 3): "Status Capacity is determined by the person's status as, for example, someone who is old, has an intellectual disability or dementia, has speech problems, has had a stroke"; "Professionals are mostly aware that assessments based on status should be avoided because they are unfairly discriminatory".
claims.location: Stipinovich abstract (Background); Kim abstract (Purpose); Hughes 2015 full text, Box 3 and 'Approaches to assessment'
claims.pico_timeframe: People with post-stroke aphasia; general principle of capacity assessment
claims.safe_wording: After a stroke, some people lose words but may keep their judgement. Aphasia can hide a person's ability to decide. Some people with aphasia also have problems with memory or reasoning, so the answer comes from a supported assessment, not from the diagnosis.
claims.qualifications: Use 'may keep their judgement', never 'keep' (judge's note). Always pair with the point that some people with aphasia also have wider cognitive problems.
claims.conflicting_or_uncertain: Non-linguistic cognitive deficits are common in post-stroke aphasia (seen in Consensus discovery results, not opened or used for a figure); do not state a proportion.

claims.claim: In a small study, people with aphasia did worse than matched controls on a language-based decision task but did not differ clearly on non-verbal decision tasks.
claims.supporting_passage: PWA differed significantly from control participants on linguistic decision making, particularly when required to verbalize their rationale for making their decision. PWA and control participants did not differ significantly on measures of nonlinguistic decision making. ... Decision-making tasks that are heavily dependent on language, such as those used in capacity assessments, may disadvantage PWA. Assessments of decision-making capacity should include communication supports for people with acquired communication disorders
claims.location: Abstract, Results and Conclusions
claims.pico_timeframe: 16 people with aphasia vs 16 age- and education-matched controls / linguistic vs nonlinguistic decision tasks / cross-sectional
claims.safe_wording: In a study of 16 people with aphasia, they struggled most when a decision task relied on words, especially explaining their reasons aloud. On decision tasks without words, they did not score clearly differently from people without aphasia.
claims.qualifications: Small study; laboratory tasks, not real capacity assessments; 'did not differ significantly' is not proof of equal ability.
claims.conflicting_or_uncertain: Small sample limits power to detect differences on nonlinguistic tasks.

numbers.meaning: people with aphasia and matched controls

claims.claim: Communication supports (information in several forms, trained partners, extra time) can help people with aphasia take part in decisions.
claims.supporting_passage: Decision-making by persons with aphasia (PWA) can be enhanced when communication partners are trained and if communication supports are provided, for example, supports that reduce the linguistic and cognitive demands of the task, and/or that facilitate expression. ... The most frequently listed strategies include augmenting information with different modalities, acknowledging the competence of the PWA, thereby inviting initiation and collaboration by the PWA, and the allocation of sufficient time for the decision-making process. ... Future research should focus on the effectiveness of the different strategies identified
claims.location: Abstract (Background, Outcomes & Results, Conclusions)
claims.pico_timeframe: 16 studies of people with post-stroke aphasia making decisions (mostly discharge, accommodation, research consent) / communication strategies / 1998 to 2021
claims.safe_wording: Research on people with aphasia after stroke describes supports that help: key words written down, pictures of the options, trained conversation partners and more time.
claims.qualifications: The review maps strategies; effectiveness of individual strategies is not established. Say 'can help', not 'proven to'. 'Key words written down' and 'pictures' are examples of 'augmenting information with different modalities'.
claims.conflicting_or_uncertain: Evidence base small (16 articles), mostly descriptive.

numbers.meaning: articles in the scoping review

claims.claim: In an international survey of 195 speech and language therapists, barriers to supporting decision-making for people with aphasia included other disciplines not seeking their involvement.
claims.supporting_passage: One hundred ninety-five SLTs from 32 countries responded. Most respondents, especially those working in inpatient settings, had supported people with aphasia to make decisions as part of a general conversation or had enabled other professionals to provide decision-making support, including during capacity assessments. Fewer had been involved directly in capacity assessments. ... There are barriers to SLTs being able to provide this support, for example, other disciplines not seeking their involvement in decision-making processes.
claims.location: Abstract (Results; Implications for rehabilitation)
claims.pico_timeframe: 195 speech and language therapists, 32 countries / self-reported practice and barriers / cross-sectional online survey, published 2026
claims.safe_wording: In a 2026 survey of 195 speech and language therapists in 32 countries, one barrier they reported was that other professionals did not ask for their help with decisions.
claims.qualifications: Self-selected respondents reporting their views; no proportion is given in the abstract, so do not say 'most' or 'often' for this barrier.
claims.conflicting_or_uncertain: Survey reflects therapists' perceptions, not audit data.

numbers.meaning: speech and language therapists who responded
countries

claims.claim: Health professionals without speech and language therapy training had difficulty identifying communication difficulties before capacity assessments.
claims.supporting_passage: Professionals reported they chose not to use the tool when they perceived patients' communication to be intact. Four of eight patients with a diagnosis of dementia or memory impairment, who professionals elected not to screen, were found to have significant communication needs. ... This study highlights that non-speech and language therapist health professionals have difficulty identifying and screening for communication difficulties.
claims.location: Abstract (Outcomes & Results; Conclusions & Implications)
claims.pico_timeframe: 21 professionals and 17 patients with stroke or cognitive impairment / communication screening before capacity assessment / acute and intermediate care, England
claims.safe_wording: In one English study, staff skipped communication screening when they thought a patient's communication was fine; half of the unscreened patients with dementia or memory problems (4 of 8) turned out to have significant communication needs.
claims.qualifications: Very small numbers (4 of 8); present as counts, not a percentage. The finding concerns patients with dementia or memory impairment, not only aphasia.
claims.conflicting_or_uncertain: Small case series.

numbers.meaning: unscreened patients with dementia or memory impairment found to have significant communication needs
professionals and patients in the study

claims.claim: UK capacity law requires help with communication before concluding incapacity: in England and Wales, all practicable steps to help the person decide; in Scotland, an inability to communicate that can be overcome with human or mechanical aids is not incapacity.
claims.supporting_passage: Hughes 2015 (quoting MCA 2005 s1): "A person is not to be treated as unable to make a decision unless all practicable steps to help him to do so have been taken without success." Hughes 2015: "They must be able to hear and see adequately; if special means of communication are required, these should be available; and so on. In keeping with the principles of the MCA (Box 1), 'all practicable steps' must be taken to help the person make a decision." Orr 2018: "A person must be given all practicable help to make their own decision before being treated as lacking capacity." Edwardson 2018: "This incapacity must be resulting from a mental disorder or inability to communicate because of physical disability. If this inability to communicate can be overcome with human or mechanical aids, it does not constitute incapacity for the purposes of the Act."
claims.location: Hughes 2015 full text, Box 1 and 'Delirium, time and the UN Convention'; Orr 2018 full text, Table 2; Edwardson 2018 full text, 'Mental capacity in Scots law'
claims.pico_timeframe: Statute as quoted in peer-reviewed secondary sources: MCA 2005 s1 (England and Wales); Adults with Incapacity (Scotland) Act 2000 s1
claims.safe_wording: In England and Wales the law says a person can't be treated as unable to decide until all practicable steps to help them have failed. In Scotland, a communication difficulty that can be overcome with help or aids does not count as incapacity.
claims.qualifications: Statutes were not opened directly; wording rests on published secondary sources quoting them. The Scottish provision concerns inability to communicate; where aphasia affects understanding, the general principles apply rather than this clause. The editor set aside posts resting only on statute text, so keep this as one supporting line alongside the empirical claims.
claims.conflicting_or_uncertain: None.

claims.claim: A validated screening tool exists to identify stroke survivors' communication support needs before a capacity assessment.
claims.supporting_passage: This unique screening tool for stroke survivors' communication support needs during mental capacity assessments is valid and reliable. Minor refinements to administration training will improve fidelity of use.
claims.location: Abstract, Conclusions
claims.pico_timeframe: 47 community-dwelling stroke survivors, 10 SLTs; 5 stroke staff and 8 inpatients for fidelity; north-west England; 2026
claims.safe_wording: A screening tool now exists to help non-specialist staff spot which stroke survivors need communication support before a capacity assessment.
claims.qualifications: Optional. Small samples; discriminant validity was poor. Do not call it 'the standard'.
claims.conflicting_or_uncertain: Early evidence only.

numbers.meaning: stroke survivors in psychometric testing

claims.claim: Under the Mental Capacity Act 2005, a person is unable to decide if, because of an impairment of mind or brain, they can't understand, retain, use or weigh the relevant information, or communicate the decision.
claims.supporting_passage: The person will be unable to make the required decision if, owing to the impairment or disturbance, he or she is unable to understand, retain, use or weigh the relevant information or to communicate the decision (MCA: section 3).
claims.location: Hughes 2015 full text, 'Context'
claims.pico_timeframe: Statute (England and Wales) as quoted in a peer-reviewed review
claims.safe_wording: The capacity test in England and Wales asks whether the person can understand, retain, use or weigh the information, and communicate a decision.
claims.qualifications: England and Wales only; the Act was not opened directly.
claims.conflicting_or_uncertain: None.

claims.claim: Some people with frontal or executive impairment can describe what they would do but fail to do it in everyday life (the 'frontal lobe paradox').
claims.supporting_passage: The "frontal lobe paradox" highlights a phenomenon in which a subset of patients who possess frontal lobe damage and exhibit marked impairments in everyday life are still able to able to verbally describe a logical course of action relating to a task and perform well in interview and test settings. Such cases pose a challenge with regard to the assessment of mental capacity within clinical settings. ... Nearly 50% of all identified academic texts published since 2000 were position articles that cited a handful of case studies published between 1936 and 1986 as evidence for the phenomenon. ... Overall, our findings indicate a lack of readily accessible research specific to the frontal lobe paradox. In particular, there is a lack of contemporary research specific to the subject and an absence of clarification as to which syndromes and disorders are included within the term.
claims.location: Abstract
claims.pico_timeframe: 28 documents on the frontal lobe paradox / scoping review / literature to 2022
claims.safe_wording: Some people with damage to the brain's planning systems can describe a task well in interview yet struggle to do it in daily life. The label for this, the 'frontal lobe paradox', is widely cited, but a 2022 review found it rests mostly on a handful of case reports from 1936 to 1986.
claims.qualifications: The phenomenon is described, not measured: no frequency, no evidence specific to older people or dementia. Do not use the label as if it were an established diagnosis. The candidate's phrase 'often with impairment of planning and self-monitoring' should become 'some people'.
claims.conflicting_or_uncertain: Position articles (e.g. George and Gilbert 2018, not opened) state the phenomenon is well known; the scoping review disputes the evidence base.

numbers.meaning: documents reviewed
publication years of the case studies commonly cited as evidence

claims.claim: Everyday decision-making ability in older people with cognitive impairment relates to executive function (ACED validation).
claims.safe_wording: Do not use.
claims.qualifications: Not searched in this batch to conserve usage; the lead (Lai 2008, ACED) was marked 'unsure' by the candidate.
claims.conflicting_or_uncertain: Unverified.

claims.claim: The Court of Protection has linked a deficit in executive functioning to inability to 'use or weigh' information, although how is unclear.
claims.supporting_passage: In a later case, NCC v PB and TB [2014] EWCOP 14, a deficit in executive functioning was tied to the inability to 'use or weigh', but the nature of this relation remains unclear.
claims.location: Ruck Keene 2019 full text, Discussion
claims.pico_timeframe: Single Court of Protection judgment, 2014, as analysed in a review of 40 dispute cases
claims.safe_wording: At least one Court of Protection judgment has tied problems with executive function to the 'use or weigh' part of the test, but legal commentators say the link is not yet clear.
claims.qualifications: One named case via a secondary source; the judgment was not opened. Do not say 'courts recognise executive capacity' as settled law.
claims.conflicting_or_uncertain: The 39 Essex Chambers guidance note was not reachable.

claims.claim: For decisions about where to live, the person should be told what the concerns are (what has gone wrong or been observed), so observations from a practical assessment are information to put to the person, not a verdict.
claims.supporting_passage: Box 4: "The person should know why a change of residence is being proposed: what have the problems been that have caused a concern (e.g. they should know why they had to come into hospital or what has caused a worry in the community)". Vignette: "An occupational therapy assessment in the ward kitchen showed that he was unsafe making a pot of tea." "From the information presented it is not possible to say with any certainty whether or not they have residence capacity. Careful assessments will be required to determine whether they do or not."
claims.location: Hughes 2015 full text, Box 4 and 'Case vignettes'
claims.pico_timeframe: Expert recommendation for residence-capacity assessment (England and Wales)
claims.safe_wording: A failed kitchen assessment does not by itself show that someone lacks capacity. Specialists recommend telling the person what the concerns are, then seeing whether they can weigh them.
claims.qualifications: The OT kitchen example in the source is a fictional teaching vignette; label any visual 'Illustrative example'.
claims.conflicting_or_uncertain: None.

claims.claim: Capacity is judged for a particular decision at a particular time; a person may lack capacity for one decision and still be able to make others.
claims.supporting_passage: Orr 2018: "A patient may lack capacity to make decisions about some aspects of their care but retain the capacity to make decisions about more straightforward aspects." "This decision confirms that capacity is time-and decision-specific and can fluctuate." Hughes 2015 (quoting MCA 2005 s2): "'a person lacks capacity in relation to a matter if at the material time he is unable to make a decision for himself in relation to the matter because of an impairment of, or a disturbance in, the functioning of, the mind or brain' (MCA: section 2)." Ruck Keene 2019 abstract: "The subject P was determined to have capacity in 13 cases, to lack capacity in 22 cases, and in 5 cases P was found to have and lack capacity for different issues before the court."
claims.location: Orr 2018 full text ('Consent: ethical principles'; 'Capacity: evolution of case law'); Hughes 2015 full text, 'Context'; Ruck Keene 2019 abstract
claims.pico_timeframe: UK capacity law as described in peer-reviewed secondary sources; 40 Court of Protection dispute cases, 2007 to 2017
claims.safe_wording: Capacity is judged one decision at a time. Someone who can't decide where to live may still be able to decide what to wear, what to eat and who visits. Courts have found the same person able to make some decisions and not others.
claims.qualifications: Everyday examples (what to wear, eat, who visits) are illustrations consistent with the principle, not quoted from the sources. The Scottish Act (AWI 2000) was not shown in opened sources to use identical decision-specific wording; say 'UK capacity law' only for the general principle stated by Orr 2018.
claims.conflicting_or_uncertain: None.

numbers.meaning: disputed cases in which the person was found to have capacity for some issues and lack it for others

claims.claim: People must be given all practicable help to make their own decisions before being treated as lacking capacity.
claims.supporting_passage: Orr 2018: "A person must be given all practicable help to make their own decision before being treated as lacking capacity." Hughes 2015 (quoting MCA s1): "A person is not to be treated as unable to make a decision unless all practicable steps to help him to do so have been taken without success."
claims.location: Orr 2018 full text, Table 2; Hughes 2015 full text, Box 1
claims.pico_timeframe: MCA 2005 principles (England and Wales) as quoted
claims.safe_wording: The law in England and Wales says people must be given all practicable help to make their own decisions. So a follow-up question is: what help will she get to make the others?
claims.qualifications: England and Wales statute via secondary sources.
claims.conflicting_or_uncertain: None.

claims.claim: Under the Adults with Incapacity (Scotland) Act 2000, anyone acting must take account of the adult's past and present wishes (s1(4)) and encourage the adult to use existing skills (s1(5)).
claims.supporting_passage: This states that an intervention carried out under the Act: (i) should achieve a benefit not otherwise achievable; (ii) is the least restrictive option (i.e. the action made or decision taken should be the minimum necessary to achieve the intended purpose); (iii) account is taken of past and present expressed wishes and feelings as far as this is practicable; (iv) there is consultation with another specified person as far as is reasonable and practicable.
claims.location: Edwardson 2018 full text, 'Mental capacity in Scots law'
claims.pico_timeframe: AWI (Scotland) Act 2000 s1 principles as summarised in a peer-reviewed review
claims.safe_wording: In Scotland, anyone acting for an adult under the Act must take account of the person's past and present wishes and feelings.
claims.qualifications: The 'past and present wishes' principle is supported. The s1(5) principle (encouraging the adult to use existing skills) is not stated in the opened source and should be left out.
claims.conflicting_or_uncertain: Scottish sources for s1(5) found by search were paywalled.

candidates.reason: The MMSE bands and likelihood ratios are confirmed word for word in the Sessums 2011 JAMA abstract (below 20: LR 6.3; 20 to 24: LR 0.87, 'no effect'; above 24: LR 0.14). Kim and Caine 2002 corroborates for 21 to 25, in research consent. Decision-specific capacity is supported by Orr 2018 and Poole 2014. Conditions: say 'treatment decisions'; say the MMSE was not designed for capacity; add the judge's point that a score above 24 lowers but does not rule out incapacity; don't transfer the cut-offs to MoCA or ACE-III; don't compute probabilities; no measured claim about executive impairment.

CC v KK facts and outcome come from Hughes 2015 (full text). The para 68 words ('The person under evaluation must be presented with detailed options so that their capacity to weigh up those options can be fairly assessed') are quoted verbatim in Ruck Keene 2019, so the judge's wording is quoted, not paraphrased. Hughes 2015 Box 4 supports presenting options with the help attached and stating the care home option honestly, which meets the judge's sharpen. Practice gaps come from Emmett 2013 (full text, dementia, residence capacity) and, as illustration only, Foulkes 2024 (acquired brain injury, 4 recordings). Conditions: name it as a first-instance England and Wales judgment; attribute the para 68 quote; describe Foulkes' population correctly; don't claim how often assessments omit options.

Aphasia frequency (median 30% acute, 34% rehabilitation) is confirmed in the Flowers 2016 systematic review. That aphasia can hide decision-making ability and that some people also have cognitive deficits is in Stipinovich 2023 and Kim 2020; Kim 2020 gives direct small-study evidence that language-heavy decision tasks disadvantage people with aphasia. The Jayes 2026 survey (195 SLTs, 32 countries) names 'other disciplines not seeking their involvement' as a barrier. Jayes 2020 shows non-specialists miss communication needs. The legal duty to help comes from published secondary sources. Conditions: use 'may keep their judgement'; give no proportion for the survey barrier; say supports 'can help', since effectiveness isn't tested; give one action: ask the speech and language therapist before the capacity conversation.

Reserve. The core empirical claim, that people with executive impairment describe tasks well but fail to do them, rests on a contested label. The Newstead 2022 scoping review found the evidence is mostly position articles citing case studies from 1936 to 1986. The ACED claim was not verified. One named judgment (NCC v PB and TB [2014] EWCOP 14) is available only through Ruck Keene 2019, which says the link to 'use or weigh' is unclear. The 'show as well as tell' step is supportable only as expert recommendation (Hughes 2015), framed as information to put to the person.
candidates.revised_angle: Reading the evidence or Teaching round: the 'frontal lobe paradox' is widely taught in capacity training, but a 2022 scoping review found it rests mostly on a handful of case reports from 1936 to 1986. Courts have linked executive problems to the 'use or weigh' test in at least one case, but the link is unclear. The practical point still holds as good practice: what you see in a kitchen assessment is information to put to the person, then you see whether they can weigh it. It is not a verdict on capacity. Any kitchen scenario must be labelled 'Illustrative example'.

candidates.reason: Reserve. Decision-specific capacity and the duty to give all practicable help are supported (Orr 2018; Hughes 2015 quoting MCA ss1 and 2; Ruck Keene 2019: 5 of 40 disputed cases found capacity for some issues and not others). The AWI s1(5) 'encourage skills' claim was not found in an opened source and must be dropped; only the AWI 'past and present wishes' principle can be used for Scotland. The judge's follow-up question ('What help will she get to make the others?') is supported by the all-practicable-steps principle. Everyday examples are illustrations, not quoted.
